newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor edges to victory in Liberia poll.
newsitem.headline: Taylor edges to victory in Liberia poll.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor extended his lead in Liberia's elections on Monday, edging towards a victory through the ballot box that he failed to achieve by the gun.
Election Commission chief Harry Andrews said that with one third of potential votes counted, Taylor had just under 66 percent of valid votes cast, up from 62 percent on Sunday.
Taylor's closest rival, former senior U.N. official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the field of 12, saw her tally fall from 18 percent to less than 16 percent.
Monday newspapers in the capital Monrovia headlined the lead of the man who plunged the West African nation into a seven-year civil war when he invaded from Ivory Coast in 1989.
Johnson-Sirleaf and her Unity Party cried foul but foreign election observers gave the poll a clean bill of health.

Johnson-Sirleaf said unauthorised people helped some voters. "People did not know how to vote in many areas and needed assistance. During that assistance their intent and wishes were not respected," she told state radio.

Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter said most problems his team had seen stemmed from general ignorance on how to vote. "These problems or irregularities did not have a pattern and did not affect the outcome of the elections," he said.
Other foreign observers agreed.
Taylor needs 50 percent plus to avoid an August 2 run-off.
Johnson-Sirleaf's allegations of fraud, first aired on radio by her campaign manager Dusty Wolokolie on Sunday, were the first sour note in elections praised by monitors.
Wolokolie accused officials of the Independent Elections Commission and troops of the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG of interfering with voting at some stations.
"We've heard of widespread fraud on the part of IENEC officials as well as ECOMOG personnel...We have film to show evidence of ECOMOG casting ballots for people," Wolokolie said.
With 219,754 votes counted on Monday, Taylor had 144,981 or 65.97 percent. Johnson-Sirleaf had 34,914 or 15.88 percent.
Wolokolie was interviewed live on radio from commission headquarters before Andrews broadcast first preliminary results.
ECOMOG soldiers, reacting to the interview, halted the broadcast, forcing Andrews to suspend his statement briefly.

General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led force, confirmed the action of the soldiers but said they had acted beyond their orders. "They were only told to bring the man (Wolokolie) to substantiate his allegations," Malu told Reuters.
Taylor supporters, chanting "Taylor has won" poured into the streets of Monrovia, darkened by a long-term nationwide electricity blackout, after hearing Sunday's first results.
International election experts helping with organisation estimated voter turnout on Saturday at around 85 percent.
A total of just over 700,000 people registered to vote.
Taylor is seen by many as the forceful leader needed in the post-war period. He had superior resources to his rivals. With a national radio station, he ran a well-oiled campaign machine.
Johnson-Sirleaf entered the race late but built up support through her image of integrity and good contacts with donors.
Two other former warlords, Alhaji Kromah and George Boley, also ran. Kromah was in third place with 4.29 percent.
Liberia's West African neighbours, who finally rallied the warlords around a peace deal, earlier joined the international observers in praising the smooth conduct of the poll.
